title: I used coding agents to build a turn-based BJJ game, and multiplayer was the hardest part
author: patrickcarmo
selftext:
I’ve been building BJJ DOJO, a free browser game where Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu positions are the combat states. It uses plain JavaScript and Three.js, with 45 paired techniques, IK, stamina, scoring, belt progression and tournaments.



My workflow uses Codex and Claude as coding agents. I define the behavior and constraints, keep the architecture and tests in the repo, and review the result in the browser. For the grappling animations, each technique is broken into timed steps for both fighters, then I check anatomy, anchors and collisions instead of accepting a one-shot animation.



The newest part is online multiplayer. One player creates a room, shares an invite link, and both devices play the same turn-based match. The agents helped implement and review the network flow, while I tested the actual room, mobile layout and failure cases.



It is live here: [https://bjj.patrickcarmo.com/?lang=en](https://bjj.patrickcarmo.com/?lang=en)



I’m curious how other AI game developers structure agent handoffs for systems where visual correctness matters as much as automated tests.

comments.author: Kasonanvu
comments.body: Hey this is amazing. As someone interest in BJJ, it's really cool as entertainment but also fun little education. I can see BJJ fans enjoying this

replies.author: patrickcarmo
replies.body: Thank you! That mix is exactly what I was hoping for. I wanted it to be fun first, but still leave you recognizing positions and transitions after a few fights. Really glad that came through.
